By Tom Bateman State department correspondent Published 18 August 2026 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced sanctions against the president and a senior lawyer of the International Criminal Court (ICC). The move is the Trump administration's latest escalation in its campaign to "dismantle" the court which is empowered by more than 120 member countries to investigate war crimes. Rubio said the US was sanctioning ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan and ICC Senior Trial Lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal for engaging in the ICC's efforts to "prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction". The ICC said it stands behind its staff and believes that measures such as those announced by Rubio "undermine the rule of law." Rubio accused the court of being "a corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty." Neither President Trump nor the White House has so far commented. The Trump administration has already announced sanctions on at least 11 ICC officials, including nine judges and the chief prosecutor. The sanctions include asset freezes, travel bans, and restrictions on services from U.S. companies. Those sanctions were issued in retaliation for ICC investigations into US personnel in Afghanistan and for warrants the court issued against top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for alleged war crimes in Gaza. Netanyahu has denied allegations of war crimes and accused the court of being motivated by antisemitism. Neither the US nor Israel are members of the ICC. However, the state of Palestine became a member of the ICC in 2015, opening the way for the court's examination of crimes alleged to have been committed on Palestinian territory. Trump's opposition to the court dates back to his first term in office, when he first described the ICC as a "threat" and told the UN General Assembly that it has "no jurisdiction, no legitimacy, and no authority" as far as the US is concerned. Last month, Rubio called on the ICC's 125 member countries to withdraw from the court as part of a US government campaign to dismantle it "brick by brick". Amid a growing pressure campaign, a US official said Washington would "watch with interest" who heeded its call and who did not. The ICC, which was established in 2002, has â international jurisdiction to prosecute genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes in member states or if a situation is referred by the UN Security Council. "Measures targeting judges, prosecutors and staff who work towards the fulfilment of the mandate that was conferred to the ICC by States undermine the rule of law," the court said in its statement on Tuesday. "When judicial actors are threatened for applying the law, it is the international legal order itself that is placed at risk." Rights organisations have pushed back against what they view as the Trump administration's attempts to undermine international law and stifle efforts to combat impunity by governments around the world. "The Trump administration seeks a get-out-of-jail-free card for whomever it chooses," said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch, during a press conference last week. Evenson's comments came as four leading US human rights groups sued the Trump administration over its campaign to dismantle the ICC, calling it unconstitutional. Human Rights Watch, â the Open Society Institute, the American Friends Service Committee and the Center for Constitutional Rights said in their lawsuit filed in New York that the sanctions prevented them from working with the court to seek justice for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity around the world. In June, three ICC judges also sued the administration in a New York federal court over sanctions imposed on them last year, arguing the measures were unlawful. Judges Kimberly Prost of Canada, Solomy Balungi Bossa of Uganda and Reine Alapini-Gansou of Benin said the sanctions were designed to exert extrajudicial pressure with the objective of punishing and coercing the judges. At the time, a White House official said that Trump had lawfully exercised his authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) in imposing the sanctions. Sanctions severely hamper individuals' abilities to carry out even routine financial transactions as any banks with ties to the US, or that conduct transactions in dollars, are expected to have to comply with the restrictions. Since Trump returned to office, his administration - spearheaded by Rubio - has taken a much more aggressive stand towards the court. In a July video statement announcing the campaign to dismantle the court, Rubio accused the ICC of "waging a war against our country" with "statutes, compacts and the force of so-called international law". "Today, it threatens every aspect of our political and legal system," he added. "If they believe they can deprive us of our sovereignty, we will teach them the full meaning of American resolve." http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/07/iaea-.text: The UN's nuclear watchdog said Iran had provided no information about its declared nuclear materials or facilities and that inspectors had no on-site verification access, as Tehran threatened retaliation against South Korea if Seoul joined Gulf maritime operations and Iran's parliament speaker warned US energy assets across regional waters faced reciprocal strikes.IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the agency's Board of Governors that Iran was not meeting its Non-Proliferation Treaty safeguards obligations and called for constructive engagement to restore full oversight.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei dismissed the IAEA reports as instruments of Western political pressure and warned Tehran would take countermeasures if a new resolution referred Iran's nuclear file back to the UN Security Council.He attributed restrictions on IAEA inspectors to US and Israeli strikes on Iranian enrichment infrastructure.Grossi also argued that Western efforts to revive UN Security Council oversight implicitly validated Iran, China and Russia's position that the snapback sanctions mechanism was illegal. "It is a mistake to test what has already been tested," he said.Hormuz corridor near completionBaghaei said bilateral talks with Oman on a temporary safe transit corridor in the Strait of Hormuz were near completion and would likely be registered with the International Maritime Organisation within days."We can now say that talks between Iran and Oman have reached their final stage," he said.However, the IRGC Navy's political deputy said safe passage through the US-designated southern corridor was practically impossible."Any vessel entering this corridor will no longer be safe from strikes once it reaches the area of Khasab, Oman," the official, identified as Mohammadi, said.He said the IRGC maintained continuous intelligence and operational monitoring of vessel movements across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman.Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, announced the establishment of an "exclusion zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz, extending from the US naval blockade line into the Persian Gulf."Any ship entering this area without Iran's permission and coordination will have its details — along with the names of its owner and charterer — registered and placed on Iran's sanctions list," he said.Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf separately warned on social media that US oil and gas assets across regional waters were exposed to retaliatory strikes.South Korea warnedBaghaei warned South Korea that any military presence in Gulf operations would be treated as direct support for US aggression.He framed the warning in diplomatic terms, noting that Iran-South Korea relations spanned more than 64 years and were based on mutual respect."The military presence of any other country or its participation in operations in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz will be regarded as direct support for the perpetrators of this aggression and will have serious consequences," Baghaei said.South Korea's foreign ministry said Seoul was in close contact with the international community over the situation in the Middle East and was working to help restore stability and ensure free passage through the strait for all vessels including its own.

If you are unable to attend these in-person auditions, you may submit a video audition at: https://airtable.com/appflzWBb... . CONTRACT SPT $642 weekly minimum (SPT 6) SEEKING Equity actors for roles in BILOXI BLUES (See breakdown). All roles are open to all ethnicities. PREPARATION Please prepare a 90-second monologue in the style of the show. Also, please bring your headshot and resume to the audition. LOCATION Addison Theatre Centre 15650 Addison Rd Addison, TX 75001-3285 PARKING: Use the Admin Entrance located off Morris Ave. There is free parking at the building in the back parking lot and there will be signs in the building directing you to the audition room. PERSONNEL Stage Manager: Elise Fuselier Expected to attend: Director: Penny Maas Producing Artistic Director: JC Schuster Artistic Coordinator: Zarina Izel Garza OTHER DATES Callbacks: October 11 - by invitation Rehearsals Between 01/12/2027-01/31/2027 Performances: 02/02/2027-02/14/2027 OTHER https://www.watertowertheatre.... An Equity Monitor will not be provided. The producer will run all aspects of this audition. Equity’s contracts prohibit discrimination. Equity is committed to diversity and encourages all its employers to engage in a policy of equal employment opportunity designed to promote a positive model of inclusion. As such, Equity encourages performers of all ethnicities, gender identities, and ages, as well as performers with disabilities, to attend every audition. Always bring your Equity Membership card to auditions. Breakdown BILOXI BLUES WaterTower Theatre is dedicated to diversity and inclusion as a core value, and as such we encourage actors of all ethnicities and gender identities to audition. In reference to the character descriptions below—most characters we encounter currently are on the binary and are written with he/him or she/her pronouns and you will see that in the following descriptions. But however limiting the descriptions are, our casting seeks to be as inclusive as possible and we invite gender non-conforming, genderqueer, transgender and non-binary actors to submit for the roles they most identify with. We will also list race/ethnicity when specific to the character but are otherwise seeking all races and ethnicities. Let us know if you have any questions, concerns, or if there are any accommodations we can provide (from language developed by Kevin Kantor and Emily Tarquin from the Actors Theatre of Louisville) SYNOPSIS: Part of Neil Simon's Eugene trilogy, Biloxi Blues centers on the experiences of a young army recruit, Eugene Morris Jerome, during World War II. At basic training in Biloxi, Mississippi, Eugene is determined to use his army experiences to help his writing career and keeps detailed memoirs about his experiences. Eugene and his fellow soldiers-in-training suffer under a hard-nosed drill sergeant, Merwin J. Toomey; attempt to stomach the terrible army food served up in the mess hall; and bond over an adventure to visit the local prostitute. Along the way, Eugene is forced to learn about authority, danger, assimilation, bigotry, and love. In the process, he discovers that life can be both ugly and tender. Casting Note: The roles in Biloxi Blues at WaterTower Theatre welcome performers of all gender identities to audition. Casting will be based on storytelling ability and the needs of the production. SEEKING: Eugene Jerome: 18. The protagonist and narrator. A bright, observant, somewhat neurotic young Jewish recruit from Brooklyn who dreams of becoming a writer. Eugene is inexperienced with women and the military but possesses a sharp wit and strong imagination. He grows considerably throughout the play. Sgt. Merwin J. J. Toomey: 30s–40s. The company's intimidating, authoritarian drill sergeant. Tough, volatile, crude, and seemingly heartless, Toomey uses humiliation and fear to control the recruits. Beneath his harsh exterior, however, there are glimpses of vulnerability and desperation. Joseph Wykowski: 18–20. A loud, aggressive Polish-American recruit. Physically imposing and openly prejudiced, Wykowski frequently clashes with Eugene. He represents much of the macho culture and immaturity of the barracks. Arnold B. Epstein: 18–20. An intelligent, principled Jewish recruit who becomes one of Eugene's closest friends. Thoughtful, argumentative, and politically aware, Epstein is less willing than the others to blindly follow authority. He has a strong moral compass and a dry sense of humor. Don Carney: 18–20. A good-natured, somewhat simple-minded recruit. Carney is friendly and eager to fit in. He provides humor and often gets caught up in the antics and conflicts of the barracks. James Hennesey: 18–20. A nervous, religious young recruit who struggles with the realities of military life. More innocent and sheltered than some of the others, Hennesey is often the target of teasing and intimidation. Roy Selridge: 18–20. A cocky, sexually experienced recruit who enjoys telling stories and presenting himself as worldly. He is energetic, mischievous, and often contributes to the barracks' crude humor and sexual conversations. Rowena: 18-25. A prostitute whom the soldiers encounter in a local house of prostitution. Daisy Hannigan: 18–20. A young woman Eugene meets while stationed in Biloxi. Intelligent, confident, and sexually liberated, Daisy is much more worldly than Eugene. Their relationship gives Eugene an opportunity to experience romance and adulthood outside the barracks. SALARY SPT $642 weekly minimum (SPT 6) UNION AEA

https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/men.text: Anger was growing on Sunday at Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank after European diplomats and an American journalist were caught up in the unrest. Visitors from France, Belgium and Poland were among those targeted by masked settlers near the village of Taybeh on Saturday. It came a day after Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine suffered serious injuries when she was attacked by Israeli settlers. The EU on Sunday demanded “effective measures” from Israel to stop the unrest. Poland said the attack in Taybeh, a Christian village, was evidence of what Palestinians in the West Bank face on a daily basis. “The attack should be met with a firm response from the Israeli authorities,” the Polish Foreign Ministry said. US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee demanded arrests and the prosecution of those responsible after the attack on the journalist. “Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Mr Huckabee said in a post on X early on Sunday. “Dishonourable act of senseless violence.” The US envoy said Ms Levine had been clearly identified as a journalist and was unarmed. He called for those involved to spend years in prison and demanded prosecution “to the fullest extent of the law”. The Washington Post said Ms Levine was attacked when “dozens of masked settlers” set fire to shrubs and threw rocks in a “co-ordinated assault” on Palestinian olive harvesters. “She was knocked to the ground, kicked repeatedly and stripped of her cameras and phone,” the paper said. Ms Levine was later taken to hospital in Ramallah. Photos showed her lying on a trolley with a wound dressing on the left leg and a gash on her right knee, among other injuries. On Sunday, the Post welcomed the support of the US ambassador. “We appreciate the support we’ve gotten today for our photographer, Heidi Levine, after the brutal and unwarranted attack on her. We reiterate the call for action from the government. Press freedoms are a cornerstone for democracies,” editor Matt Murray wrote on X. The attack comes amid renewed international concern over Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, after European diplomats and a French mayor were assaulted by masked people in a separate incident on Saturday. Belgium criticised the attack on its consul general and the other diplomats and urged Israel to bring those responsible to justice. Poland’s Foreign Ministry said preliminary evidence indicated Israeli settlers were responsible for the assault. Polish diplomats travelling in the convoy were unharmed, the ministry said. “We expect the Israeli authorities to provide urgent and detailed explanations, identify those responsible and ensure that they are held accountable,” it added. “We also expect effective measures to be taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the mayor of a French town had also been assaulted by what he described as “extremist settlers” during Saturday’s incident. He called on Israeli authorities to stop the violence. Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Ms Levine to apologise for the attack and urged an investigation. The Israeli military described the violence as intolerable and said the incidents would be investigated. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said the circumstances remained unclear and more evidence was needed before responsibility could be established. It also noted that the diplomats’ visit had not been co-ordinated with Israeli security officials. Britain, France, Canada and other countries announced sanctions focused on Israeli settlements last month, while the US said it would not join those measures.
